claim: Microbial collectives can perform functions beyond the capability of individual members.
source: Microbial collectives can perform functions beyond the capability of individual members.
evidence: This is a general statement about microbial collectives that is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Enhancing collective functions through artificial selection is challenging.
source: Enhancing collective functions through artificial selection is, however, challenging.
evidence: This statement is supported by the context of the manuscript and references to previous work showing unimpressive outcomes.

claim: Intermediate target S frequencies are the most challenging to achieve.
source: Using simulations and analytical calculations, we show that intermediate target S frequencies are the most challenging, akin to a target within the vertical drop of a waterfall, rather than above or below it.
evidence: This claim is supported by both simulations and analytical calculations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Intra-collective selection is the strongest at intermediate S-frequencies.
source: This arises because intra-collective selection is the strongest at intermediate S-frequencies, which can overpower inter-collective selection.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analytical calculations and simulations showing the relationship between frequency and selection strength.

claim: Achieving a low target S frequency is consistently feasible.
source: While achieving a low target S frequencies is consistently feasible, attaining high target S-frequencies requires an initially high S-frequency — much like a raft that can descend but not ascend a waterfall.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations showing successful achievement of low target frequencies from various initial conditions.

claim: Attaining high target S-frequencies requires an initially high S-frequency.
source: While achieving a low target S frequencies is consistently feasible, attaining high target S-frequencies requires an initially high S-frequency — much like a raft that can descend but not ascend a waterfall.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations showing that high target frequencies can only be achieved from high initial frequencies.

claim: As Newborn size increases, the region of achievable target frequency is reduced until no frequency is achievable.
source: As Newborn size increases, the region of achievable target frequency is reduced until no frequency is achievable.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4a showing the relationship between Newborn size and achievable target frequencies.

claim: The number of collectives under selection plays a less critical role than Newborn size.
source: In contrast, the number of collectives under selection plays a less critical role.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analytical calculations and simulations comparing the effects of different parameters.

claim: In scenarios involving more than two populations, the evolutionary trajectory must navigate entirely away from the metaphorical 'waterfall drop.'
source: In scenarios involving more than two populations, the evolutionary trajectory must navigate entirely away from the metaphorical 'waterfall drop.'
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations of three-population systems shown in Figure 5.

claim: The strength of intra-collective evolution is frequency-dependent.
source: Our findings illustrate that the strength of intra-collective evolution is frequency-dependent, with implications in experimental planning.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analytical calculations and simulations showing varying selection strength at different frequencies.

claim: Microbial collectives can carry out functions such as waste degradation.
source: Microbial collectives can carry out functions that arise from interactions among member species. These functions, such as waste degradation (Woo et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2022), probiotics (Bober et al., 2018), and vitamin production (Wang et al., 2016), can be useful for human health and biotechnology.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microbial collectives can carry out functions such as probiotics.
source: Microbial collectives can carry out functions that arise from interactions among member species. These functions, such as waste degradation (Woo et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2022), probiotics (Bober et al., 2018), and vitamin production (Wang et al., 2016), can be useful for human health and biotechnology.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microbial collectives can carry out functions such as vitamin production.
source: Microbial collectives can carry out functions that arise from interactions among member species. These functions, such as waste degradation (Woo et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2022), probiotics (Bober et al., 2018), and vitamin production (Wang et al., 2016), can be useful for human health and biotechnology.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Artificial selection of collectives have been attempted in experiments.
source: Artificial selection of collectives have been attempted both in experiments (Goodnight, 1990; Swenson et al., 2000b; Swenson et al., 2000a; Blouin et al., 2015; Panke-Buisse et al., 2015; Panke-Buisse et al., 2017; Jochum et al., 2019; Wright et al., 2019; Raynaud et al., 2019; Arora et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2020; Mueller et al., 2021; Jacquiod et al., 2022; Raynaud et al., 2022; Arias-Sánchez et al., 2024) and in simulations (Penn, 2003; Penn and Harvey, 2004; Williams and Lenton, 2007; Xie et al., 2019; Doulcier et al., 2020; Xie and Shou, 2021; Chang et al., 2021; Fraboul et al., 2023; Lalejini et al., 2022; Zaccaria et al., 2023; Vessman et al., 2023), often with unimpressive outcomes.
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to experimental studies.

claim: Artificial selection of collectives have been attempted in simulations.
source: Artificial selection of collectives have been attempted both in experiments (Goodnight, 1990; Swenson et al., 2000b; Swenson et al., 2000a; Blouin et al., 2015; Panke-Buisse et al., 2015; Panke-Buisse et al., 2017; Jochum et al., 2019; Wright et al., 2019; Raynaud et al., 2019; Arora et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2020; Mueller et al., 2021; Jacquiod et al., 2022; Raynaud et al., 2022; Arias-Sánchez et al., 2024) and in simulations (Penn, 2003; Penn and Harvey, 2004; Williams and Lenton, 2007; Xie et al., 2019; Doulcier et al., 2020; Xie and Shou, 2021; Chang et al., 2021; Fraboul et al., 2023; Lalejini et al., 2022; Zaccaria et al., 2023; Vessman et al., 2023), often with unimpressive outcomes.
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to simulation studies.

claim: Artificial selection of collectives often has unimpressive outcomes.
source: Artificial selection of collectives have been attempted both in experiments (Goodnight, 1990; Swenson et al., 2000b; Swenson et al., 2000a; Blouin et al., 2015; Panke-Buisse et al., 2015; Panke-Buisse et al., 2017; Jochum et al., 2019; Wright et al., 2019; Raynaud et al., 2019; Arora et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2020; Mueller et al., 2021; Jacquiod et al., 2022; Raynaud et al., 2022; Arias-Sánchez et al., 2024) and in simulations (Penn, 2003; Penn and Harvey, 2004; Williams and Lenton, 2007; Xie et al., 2019; Doulcier et al., 2020; Xie and Shou, 2021; Chang et al., 2021; Fraboul et al., 2023; Lalejini et al., 2022; Zaccaria et al., 2023; Vessman et al., 2023), often with unimpressive outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited literature on collective selection attempts.

claim: One of the major challenges in selecting collectives is to ensure the inheritance of a collective function.
source: One of the major challenges in selecting collectives is to ensure the inheritance of a collective function (Xie et al., 2023; Thomas et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inheritance from a parent collective to offspring collectives can be compromised by changes in genotype and species compositions.
source: Inheritance from a parent collective to offspring collectives can be compromised by changes in genotype and species compositions.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the biological processes described.

claim: During maturation of a collective, genotype compositions within each species can change due to intra-collective selection favoring fast-growing individuals.
source: During maturation of a collective, genotype compositions within each species can change due to intra-collective selection favoring fast-growing individuals (Figure 1, 'intra-collective' selection), while species compositions can change due to ecological interactions.
evidence: This is based on established evolutionary principles and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Species compositions can change due to ecological interactions during collective maturation.
source: During maturation of a collective, genotype compositions within each species can change due to intra-collective selection favoring fast-growing individuals (Figure 1, 'intra-collective' selection), while species compositions can change due to ecological interactions.
evidence: This is based on established ecological principles.

claim: During the reproduction of a collective, genotype and species compositions of offspring can vary stochastically from those of the parent.
source: Furthermore, during the reproduction of a collective, genotype and species compositions of offspring can vary stochastically from those of the parent (Figure 1, 'genetic drift').
evidence: This is based on the principle of genetic drift, a well-established concept in population genetics.

claim: Whenever a collective function depends on both populations, the collective function is maximized at an intermediate frequency.
source: This is a common quest: whenever a collective function depends on both populations, the collective function is maximized, by definition, at an intermediate frequency (e.g. too little of either population will hamper function; Xie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a logical inference supported by a citation.

claim: Nearly any target species composition can be achieved when selecting communities of two competing species with unequal growth rates, so long as the shared resource is depleted during collective maturation.
source: Earlier work has demonstrated that nearly any target species composition can be achieved when selecting communities of two competing species with unequal growth rates (Doulcier et al., 2020; Rainey, 2023), so long as the shared resource is depleted during collective maturation (Doulcier et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the case of resource depletion, initially both species evolved to grow faster, and the slower-growing species was preserved due to stochastic fluctuations in species composition during collective reproduction.
source: In this case, initially, both species evolved to grow faster, and the slower-growing species was preserved due to stochastic fluctuations in species composition during collective reproduction.
evidence: This describes findings from earlier work (Doulcier et al., 2020).

claim: Eventually, both species evolved to grow sufficiently fast to deplete the shared resource during collective maturation, and evolution in competition coefficients then acted to stabilize the species ratio to the target value.
source: Eventually, both species evolved to grow sufficiently fast to deplete the shared resource during collective maturation, and evolution in competition coefficients then acted to stabilize the species ratio to the target value (Doulcier et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes findings from earlier work (Doulcier et al., 2020).

claim: Earlier studies are often limited to numerical explorations, with prohibitive costs for a full characterization of the parameter space for nested populations.
source: Regardless, earlier studies are often limited to numerical explorations, with prohibitive costs for a full characterization of the parameter space for such nested populations (population of collectives, and populations of variants within a collective).
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of previous research.

claim: The model assumes growth is always exponential, without complications such as resource limitation, ecological interactions between the two populations, or density-dependent growth.
source: First, growth is always exponential, without complications such as resource limitation, ecological interactions between the two populations, or density-dependent growth.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the model.

claim: The model does not consider a spectrum of mutants or species because with more than two populations, an analytical solution becomes very difficult.
source: We do not consider a spectrum of mutants or species, since with more than two populations, an analytical solution becomes very difficult.
evidence: This is a stated justification for a modeling choice.

claim: The single top-functioning community is chosen to reproduce, which allows the use of the simplest version of the extreme value theory.
source: Finally, the single top-functioning community is chosen to reproduce, which allows us to employ the simplest version of the extreme value theory (see section below for further justification).
evidence: This is a stated assumption and justification for the modeling approach.

claim: The model scenario is encountered in biotechnology where an engineered pathway will slow down cell growth, and breaking the pathway is much easier than the other way around.
source: We made this choice because it is more challenging to attain or maintain the target frequency when the abundance of fast-growing F is further increased via mutations. This scenario is encountered in biotechnology: an engineered pathway will slow down cell growth, and breaking the pathway (and thus faster growth) is much easier than the other way around.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of biotechnology applications.

claim: When the mutation rate is set to zero, the same model can be used to capture collectives of two species with different growth rates.
source: When the mutation rate is set to zero, the same model can be used to capture collectives of two species with different growth rates.
evidence: This is a stated property of the model.

claim: Even though S and F do not compete for nutrients, they compete for space because the total number of cells transferred to the next cycle is fixed.
source: Note that even though S and F do not compete for nutrients, they compete for space: because the total number of cells transferred to the next cycle is fixed, an overabundance of one population will reduce the likelihood of the other being propagated.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the model dynamics.

claim: Choosing top 1 is more effective than the less stringent 'choosing top 5%' in this study.
source: In contrast with findings from an earlier study (Xie et al., 2019), choosing top 1 is more effective than the less stringent 'choosing top 5%.'
evidence: This is supported by comparison with earlier work and data in Appendix 7—figure 1.

claim: In an earlier study, variation in the collective trait is partly due to nonheritable factors such as random fluctuations in Newborn biomass.
source: In the earlier study, variation in the collective trait is partly due to nonheritable factors such as random fluctuations in Newborn biomass.
evidence: This describes findings from earlier work (Xie et al., 2019).

claim: This study excludes non-heritable variations in collective traits.
source: However, since this study excludes non-heritable variations in collective traits, selecting the top 1 collective is more effective than selecting the top 5% (see Appendix 7—figure 1).
evidence: This is a stated property of the model in this study.

claim: The model considers mutational stochasticity and demographic stochasticity in terms of stochastic birth and stochastic sampling of a parent collective by offspring collectives.
source: Overall, our model considers mutational stochasticity, as well as demographic stochasticity in terms of stochastic birth and stochastic sampling of a parent collective by offspring collectives.
evidence: This is a description of the types of stochasticity included in the model.

claim: Other types of stochasticity, such as environmental stochasticity and measurement noise, are not considered and require future research.
source: Other types of stochasticity, such as environmental stochasticity and measurement noise, are not considered and require future research.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the model.

claim: Without collective-level selection, F frequency increases until F reaches fixation.
source: In contrast, without collective-level selection (e.g. choosing a random collective to reproduce), F frequency increases until F reaches fixation (Supplementary information Appendix 1—figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Appendix 1—figure 3b.

claim: If the magnitude of down-shift due to inter-collective selection exceeds that of up-shift due to intra-collective selection, progress toward the target is made.
source: If the magnitude of down-shift exceeded that of up-shift, progress toward the target was made.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the visualization in Figure 2d.

claim: When Newborn F frequency is intermediate, intra-collective selection is the strongest and may overwhelm inter-collective selection.
source: Thus, when Newborn F frequency is intermediate, intra-collective selection is the strongest and may overwhelm inter-collective selection (Figure 3b and Appendix 2—figure 2a).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3b and Appendix 2—figure 2a.

claim: Similar conclusions about the waterfall phenomenon are derived where S and F are slow-growing and fast-growing species which cannot be converted through mutations.
source: Not surprisingly, similar conclusions are derived where S and F are slow-growing and fast-growing species which cannot be converted through mutations (Appendix 4 and Appendix 4—figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Appendix 4 and Appendix 4—figure 1.

claim: A larger number of collectives broadens the region of success.
source: Thus, a larger number of collectives broadens the region of success (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4b.

claim: In the three-population case, the evolutionary trajectory travels in a two-dimensional plane.
source: In the three-population case, the evolutionary trajectory travels in a two-dimensional plane.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of having three populations with frequencies that sum to 1.

claim: A target population composition in the three-population system can be achieved if inter-collective selection can sufficiently reduce the frequencies of F as well as FF.
source: A target population composition can be achieved if inter-collective selection can sufficiently reduce the frequencies of F as well as FF (accessible regions, gold in Figure 5b).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5b.

claim: The rate at which FF grows faster than S+F is greater than the rate at which F grows faster than S in the three-population system.
source: Intuitively, the rate at which FF grows faster than S+F is greater than the rate at which F grows faster than S (see Appendix 8).
evidence: This is explained in Appendix 8.

claim: The three-population problem can initially be reduced to a two-population problem (FF versus F+S), and then expanded to a three-population problem.
source: Thus, the problem can initially be reduced to a two-population problem (i.e. FF versus F+S; Figure 5c left), and then expanded to a three-population problem (Figure 5c right).
evidence: This is illustrated in Figure 5c and explained through logical reasoning.

claim: In the three-population system, targets in the inaccessible region are never achievable.
source: Similar to the two-population case, targets in the inaccessible region are never achievable (Figure 5b ii), while those in the FF region are always achievable (Figure 5b i).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5b.

claim: In the three-population system, targets in the FF region are always achievable.
source: Similar to the two-population case, targets in the inaccessible region are never achievable (Figure 5b ii), while those in the FF region are always achievable (Figure 5b i).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5b.

claim: A target composition in an accessible region may not be achievable even when the initial composition is within the same region if the composition escapes the accessible region during evolution.
source: Strikingly, a target composition in an accessible region may not be achievable even when the initial composition is within the same region: once the composition escapes the accessible region, the trajectory cannot return back to the accessible region (Figure 5biii, the leftmost initial condition).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5b iii.

claim: If the initial position is closer to the target in the accessible region, the target becomes achievable in the three-population system.
source: However, if the initial position is closer to the target in the accessible region, the target becomes achievable (Figure 5b iii, initial condition near the bottom).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5b iii.

claim: In the three-population system, the selection outcome is path-dependent in the sense of being sensitive to initial conditions.
source: Note that here, the selection outcome is path-dependent in the sense of being sensitive to initial conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the results shown in Figure 5b iii.

claim: The path-dependence in the three-population system is distinct from hysteresis, where path-dependence results from whether a tuning parameter is increased or decreased.
source: This phenomenon is distinct from hysteresis, where path-dependence results from whether a tuning parameter is increased or decreased.
evidence: This is a clarification distinguishing the observed phenomenon from hysteresis.

claim: Strategically choosing an appropriate starting point can be essential for successful collective selection.
source: Our work suggests that the strength of intra-collective selection is not constant, and that strategically choosing an appropriate starting point can be essential for successful collective selection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of the study.

claim: The model uses the tau-leaping algorithm for stochastic simulation of cell division and mutation.
source: We can simulate the division and mutation of each individual cell stochastically by using the tau-leaping algorithm (Gillespie, 2001; Cao et al., 2006; see Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation method with citations.

claim: Individual-based simulations require a long computing time.
source: However, individual-based simulations require a long computing time.
evidence: This is a stated justification for using an alternative approach.

claim: Each distribution of S and F follows a Gaussian distribution, with the mean and variance numerically obtained from ordinary differential equations derived from the master equation.
source: Each distribution follows a Gaussian distribution, with the mean and variance numerically obtained from ordinary differential equations derived from the master equation (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a description of the analytical approach used in the model.
